title: Mixing Problems
short: Rate of change = rate in − rate out.
trouble: Students subtract the outflow rate in liters instead of the amount of salt leaving per minute.

blocks.html: Many models are careful bookkeeping. A tank of brine, a lake with a pollutant, a bloodstream with a drug: in each, an amount changes because some flows in and some flows out. Writing that balance as an equation usually gives a linear first-order equation.

Let $Q(t)$ be the amount of salt (grams), not its concentration. Then $$\frac{dQ}{dt} = \underbrace{c_{\text{in}}\,r_{\text{in}}}_{\text{rate in}} - \underbrace{\frac{Q}{V(t)}\,r_{\text{out}}}_{\text{rate out}},$$ where $c_{\text{in}}$ is the incoming concentration (g/L), $r_{\text{in}}, r_{\text{out}}$ are flow rates (L/min) and $V(t) = V_0 + (r_{\text{in}} - r_{\text{out}})t$ is the volume.

In a short time $\Delta t$, about $r_{\text{in}}\Delta t$ liters enter, carrying $c_{\text{in}}r_{\text{in}}\Delta t$ grams. The tank is well mixed, so every liter inside holds $\frac{Q}{V}$ grams, and the $r_{\text{out}}\Delta t$ liters that leave carry $\frac{Q}{V}r_{\text{out}}\Delta t$ grams. So $\Delta Q \approx \left(c_{\text{in}}r_{\text{in}} - \frac{Q}{V}r_{\text{out}}\right)\Delta t$; divide by $\Delta t$ and let it shrink. Every term is in grams per minute, a useful check.

blocks.title: Set up and solve
blocks.q: A 100 L tank holds water with 20 g of salt. Brine with 3 g/L flows in at 2 L/min, and the mixture drains at 2 L/min. Find $Q(t)$.
steps: Rate in: $3 \cdot 2 = 6$ g/min. The volume stays 100 L, so rate out: $\frac{Q}{100}\cdot 2 = \frac{Q}{50}$ g/min.
$Q' = 6 - \frac{Q}{50}$, or $Q' + \frac{1}{50}Q = 6$. The equilibrium is $Q = 300$ g (that is, 3 g/L times 100 L).

blocks.title: How long?
blocks.q: In the same tank, when does the amount reach 160 g?

blocks.title: A filling tank
blocks.q: A 100 L tank starts with 50 L of pure water. Brine with 2 g/L enters at 3 L/min, and the mixture leaves at 2 L/min. How much salt is in the tank when it is full?
steps: The volume grows by 1 L/min: $V = 50 + t$, full at $t = 50$.

blocks.html: Subtracting the outflow rate in liters, writing $Q' = 6 - 2$, mixes water with salt. The outflow of salt is (concentration in the tank) × (liters per minute), $\frac{Q}{V}r_{\text{out}}$, and it depends on $Q$. A units check catches it: grams per minute minus liters per minute does not make sense.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: $Q(t) = 300 - 280e^{-t/50}$ rises toward 300 g, the amount the tank would hold at the incoming concentration. Drag the point along the curve; at $t \approx 34.7$ it passes 160 g.
